section.title: The New Life in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Having called the church to walk worthy and grow into maturity, Paul now spells out what that new life looks like in practice. He contrasts the darkened, futile way of the Gentiles with the way believers came to know Christ, then frames the whole Christian life as a great exchange: put off the old self and put on the new, created to be like God. From that principle he draws a string of concrete commands about truth, anger, work, and speech, all shaped by love for one's neighbor and grief at grieving the Spirit. The chapter ends where the gospel begins, with kindness and forgiveness grounded in how God has forgiven us in Christ.
section.thesis: Because they have learned Christ, believers must no longer walk in the futility and corruption of the old self but put it off and put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness, living out that renewal in truthful speech, righteous anger, honest work, gracious words, and tenderhearted forgiveness that mirrors God's forgiveness of them in Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: no longer walking as the Gentiles in futility and darkness; the great exchange of putting off the old self and putting on the new; the new life worked out in truth, anger, work, and speech; and kindness and forgiveness after the pattern of God in Christ.

units.label: No longer walk as the Gentiles

verses.text: So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the {{mataiotes|futility}} of their thinking.
They are darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts.
Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more.

units.label: Put off the old self, put on the new

verses.text: But this is not the way you came to know Christ.
Surely you heard of Him and were taught in Him, in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus,
to {{apotithemi|put off}} your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires;
to be {{ananeoo|renewed}} in the spirit of your minds;
and to {{enduo|put on}} the {{kainos|new}} self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.

units.label: The new life in practice: truth, anger, work, speech

verses.text: Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another.
"Be angry, yet do not sin." Do not let the sun set upon your anger,
and do not give the devil a foothold.
He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need.
Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.
And do not {{lupeo|grieve}} the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

units.label: Kindness and forgiveness
units.note: as God in Christ forgave you

verses.text: Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice.
Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, {{aphiemi|forgiving}} each other just as in Christ God forgave you.

mataiotes.gloss: Futility, emptiness, vanity, purposelessness. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the vanity of idols and the fleeting emptiness of life apart from God. Paul says the Gentile mind runs in futility, thinking that leads nowhere because it is cut off from the life of God. The renewed mind, by contrast, is filled with the truth that is in Jesus.

apotithemi.gloss: To put off, lay aside, or strip away, as one removes and discards soiled clothing. Paul uses it for casting off the old self with its deceitful desires and for putting away falsehood. The image is of decisively taking off the garment of the former life so that it is left behind, not merely loosened while still worn.

ananeoo.gloss: To be renewed, made new again, refreshed in the inner life. It describes an ongoing renewal in the spirit of the mind, the deep reorientation of thought and desire that the Spirit works in believers. The old futile thinking is replaced as the mind is continually made new, so that the whole person is reshaped toward God.

enduo.gloss: To put on, clothe oneself with, as one dresses in a garment. Paired with putting off, it completes the picture of the great exchange: the old self is stripped away and the new self is put on. Believers are to clothe themselves with the new humanity, created to be like God, wearing a life that answers to their new identity in Christ.

kainos.gloss: New, fresh, of a new kind and quality, not merely new in time but new in nature. The new self is not a patched version of the old but a fresh creation, made to be like God in true righteousness and holiness. The word points to the newness of the new creation begun in Christ, a humanity remade after the image of its Maker.

lupeo.gloss: To grieve, cause sorrow or pain. Strikingly, Paul says sin grieves the Holy Spirit of God, treating the Spirit as a person who can be pained by the sin of those He indwells. The word reveals both the personhood of the Spirit and the closeness of His relationship to believers, in whom He dwells and by whom they are sealed for the day of redemption.

aphiemi.gloss: To forgive, release, let go, send away, cancel a debt. The same verb runs through the New Testament for God's forgiveness of sins. Here believers are to forgive one another with the very forgiveness they have received, letting go of wrongs as God in Christ has let go of theirs. Forgiveness given flows from forgiveness received.

basic.context: Paul now shows what the new life looks like in daily practice. He insists that believers must no longer live like the surrounding pagans, whose minds run in futility, whose understanding is darkened, and who have given themselves over to impurity. That is not how they learned Christ. The heart of the Christian life is a great exchange: put off the old self, which is rotting under its deceitful desires, be renewed in mind, and put on the new self, created to be like God. From there flow concrete commands, speak truth, deal with anger before it festers, work honestly and generously, use words that build others up, and do not grieve the Spirit. The chapter closes by rooting kindness and forgiveness in the forgiveness God has shown in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage moves from contrast to principle to practice. Verses 17 to 19 describe the old pagan way, verses 20 to 24 give the governing principle of putting off and putting on, and verses 25 to 32 apply it to specific areas of life. Each command is grounded in a gospel reason: we are members of one another, we are sealed by the Spirit, we have been forgiven in Christ. The imperatives are not bare rules but the working out of the new identity believers already have.
basic.originalLanguages: The Gentile mind runs in mataiotes, futility, an empty purposelessness cut off from God. Believers are to apotithemi, put off, the old self like soiled clothing, to be ananeoo, renewed, in the spirit of the mind, and to enduo, put on, the new self, which is kainos, new in kind, a fresh creation like God. Sin is serious enough to lupeo, grieve, the Holy Spirit who seals us. And the summons is to aphiemi, forgive, one another as God in Christ has forgiven us.
basic.typology: The new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness, echoes the first creation of humanity in the image of God, now restored and remade in Christ. Where Adam fell into futility and darkness, the new humanity in Christ is renewed after the likeness of its Maker, a new creation putting on what was lost in the fall.
basic.christ: The whole passage turns on knowing Christ. Believers did not learn futility and impurity; they learned Christ, were taught in Him, according to the truth that is in Jesus. The new self is put on in union with Him, and the climax grounds all forgiveness in what God has done in Christ, forgiving us so fully that we can forgive one another. Christ is both the pattern and the power of the new life.
basic.god: God is the pattern of the new humanity, which is created to be like Him in true righteousness and holiness. His Spirit indwells believers and can be grieved by their sin, showing how personal and near He is. And His forgiveness in Christ is the fountain from which all human forgiveness flows. The God who made us in His image now remakes us to be like Him and forgives us freely.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 3 gives the same picture of putting off the old self and putting on the new, created after the image of its Maker. Romans 12 calls for the renewing of the mind. Romans 6 speaks of walking in newness of life after dying to sin with Christ.
basic.oneStory: This is the renewal of the image of God in fallen humanity. Where sin darkened the mind and corrupted the heart, God is remaking a people to be like Him again, undoing the futility that followed the fall. The new self put on here is the redeemed humanity the whole story has been moving toward, a people forgiven and made new, reflecting the God who forgave them in Christ.

context.literary:
Ephesians 4:17 begins the long second half of the letter's ethical appeal, and it is built on a walking motif that has run through the whole book. Believers once 'walked' in trespasses, Ephesians 2:2, are created for good works to 'walk' in, Ephesians 2:10, and are urged to walk worthy of the calling, Ephesians 4:1. Here the verb returns, and it will return again in 5:2, 5:8 and 5:15. Paul is not adding a moral appendix to his theology; he is spelling out what the walk looks like.

The unit is built as a sandwich. Verses 17 to 19 paint the old life in four stages of decline: futile thinking, darkened understanding, alienation from God, and finally a hardened, shameless appetite. Verses 20 to 24 turn on a sharp 'But' and give the pivot of the whole chapter, two or three infinitives that are not really commands but a description of what the readers were taught. Verses 25 to 32 then work the pivot out in five concrete areas, and each command is chased by a 'because' or a 'so that', a reason drawn from the gospel.

A repeated rhythm gives the practical section its force. Almost every command pairs a negative with a positive: put off falsehood, speak truth; stop stealing, work and give; no rotten talk, only what builds up; get rid of bitterness, be kind. The pattern is a small enactment of the putting off and putting on in verses 22 to 24. Notice too how the list moves from the outward act toward the inner root, from lying to anger to stealing to speech to the Spirit's grief to the heart attitudes of verse 31, and ends on a single sentence about forgiveness that gathers all of it into the cross.
context.historical:
Paul writes as a prisoner, Ephesians 3:1 and 4:1, to churches in and around Ephesus, a great port city of Asia Minor whose life centred on the temple of Artemis. The Gentile believers there had grown up in a culture where the sexual and commercial appetites described in verse 19 were woven into religion and civic life, and Paul can speak of 'the Gentiles' in verse 17 even though most of his readers were Gentiles by birth. He is drawing a line of identity: by calling, they now belong to the people of God, no longer to the nations who do not know Him.

The list in verses 25 to 32 reads like a portrait of a close, small, vulnerable community. Lying is condemned because 'we are all members of one another', and in the life of a house church that met in homes and depended on mutual trust, falsehood did real damage. Anger that outlasted the day would sour meals shared across social lines, rich with poor, slave with free, Jew with Greek. Theft is addressed to people who had once lived by it, and Paul's remedy is not mere restraint but honest labour with a purpose, giving to the needy. That was a striking reversal in a world where manual work carried little prestige.

The command to avoid 'rotten' speech and the closing list of vices would have been familiar from Jewish wisdom teaching and from the moral lists of Greek philosophers alike. What is new is the ground. Paul does not appeal to reputation, harmony or self-improvement. He appeals to the Spirit who has sealed them and to the God who forgave them in Christ.
context.canonical:
The call to put off and put on has a close twin in Colossians 3:5 to 17, where the old self is 'put off' with its practices and the new self, being renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator, is put on. Because the two letters share so much, Ephesians 4 is best read as one of two inspired takes on the same apostolic teaching. Behind both stands Genesis 1:26 and 27, where humanity is made in God's image, and Genesis 5:1 to 3, where Adam fathers a son in his own likeness. The new self is created to be like God, Ephesians 4:24, because the first creation's purpose is being recovered.

Paul's quotation in verse 26 comes from Psalm 4:4, and the command to speak truthfully to a neighbour echoes Zechariah 8:16, spoken to a people being restored from exile. Both are drawn from the Old Testament and given a new setting in the body of Christ. The rule against theft and false speech takes up the Law, Leviticus 19:11, and Jesus' own teaching shows the same priorities: reconciliation before worship, Matthew 5:23 to 24, and the unforgiving servant who forgot how much he had been forgiven, Matthew 18:21 to 35.

The warning not to grieve the Holy Spirit recalls Isaiah 63:10, where rebellious Israel grieved God's Holy Spirit and He became their enemy. The sealing of verse 30 recalls Ephesians 1:13 to 14, the Spirit as a down payment of the inheritance. Later writers build on the same ground: Peter calls believers to put away malice and deceit, 1 Peter 2:1, and James warns that human anger does not produce the righteousness of God, James 1:19 to 20. The closing line gathers it all into the forgiveness secured at the cross, Ephesians 1:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted his readers to hear that the gospel they had received was a teaching about a way of life as much as a message about forgiveness. The phrase 'this is not the way you came to know Christ' is the heart of it: to learn Christ at all is to learn that He cannot be held alongside the old patterns. He is not offering a moral improvement programme laid over an unchanged self. He is saying that a decisive change has already happened in them, and that their daily conduct should come to match it.

He also wanted the church to see that holiness is communal. Nearly every command is framed around the neighbour: truth to the neighbour, no foothold for the devil in a shared life, work that provides for the needy, words that build up those who listen, kindness and forgiveness to one another. A person can lose their temper or lie in private, but Paul sees every such act as damage to the body.

Finally he meant to anchor all of this in grace. The last sentence does not say 'forgive because you ought' but 'forgive as God in Christ forgave you'. The readers are to work from a position of already being forgiven, sealed and renewed. Obedience is the shape that grace takes in their relationships.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is full of direct instruction, and the instructions are meant to be obeyed, not merely admired. Stop lying, deal with anger quickly, stop stealing and work, let your words build up, get rid of bitterness, forgive. These are commands to every believer in every age, and they rest on a reason Paul gives each time.

Some details need care. The line 'Be angry, yet do not sin' does not command anger as such; it grants that anger can arise and warns against letting it turn to sin or settle in for the night. The advice about the sun is a figure of speech for dealing with conflict promptly, not a rule to be kept to the minute. The instruction to the former thief describes what repentance looks like for a particular sin, and the principle applies to any habit: replace the old pattern with its opposite and give it a purpose beyond yourself.

The description of the Gentiles in verses 17 to 19 is a portrait of life without God, not a licence to despise people outside the church. Paul himself says the readers once lived that way. The same text that diagnoses the old life is, in its turn, offered as an invitation to anyone who will be taught in Jesus.

debates.question: Are 'put off' and 'put on' commands, or a statement of what has already happened?

views.label: Commands to be practised daily
views.case: The infinitives of verses 22 to 24 depend on 'you were taught', yet they read like exhortation, and the surrounding verses are plainly imperatival. Many take the three infinitives as the content of a standing instruction: keep putting off the old, keep being renewed, keep putting on the new. The present tense of 'being renewed' suggests an ongoing process.

views.label: A description of the decisive change at conversion
views.case: The parallel in Colossians 3:9 to 10 uses participles that speak of the old self as already 'put off' and the new as already 'put on'. On this reading Paul is reminding readers what they were taught, that they are people who have already made that exchange, and the commands that follow flow from the identity rather than create it.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Others hold that the two are not rivals. Paul can say you have died with Christ and also say put sin to death, Colossians 3:3 and 3:5. The identity is settled, and the daily work is to live it out.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the practical point, that conduct must change and that the change rests on what Christ has done. The disagreement shapes tone: whether a believer hears the passage mainly as encouragement to become who they are, or mainly as a summons to keep working at it. The surrounding verses support holding both.

debates.question: What does 'do not give the devil a foothold' mean in connection with anger?

views.label: Lingering anger gives Satan ground
views.case: The command follows directly after 'do not let the sun set upon your anger'. Unresolved resentment becomes a territory the enemy can occupy and use to divide the church. Paul warns elsewhere that Satan schemes to take advantage of believers, 2 Corinthians 2:10 to 11.

views.label: Any ongoing sin gives him room
views.case: The word for foothold can mean a place or opportunity, and the command stands on its own with a general scope. Anger is the nearest example, but lying, theft and rotten talk can serve the same purpose, and the rest of the chapter forms a series of ways to shut the door.

debates.bearing: The verse is a reminder that the church's moral life has an unseen opponent. Whichever scope is chosen, the instruction is the same: settle the anger and do not postpone reconciliation.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 17 opens with a pair of verbs that set the tone. Paul says 'I tell you this' and then 'insist on it in the Lord', and the second verb is the one from which we get 'martyr'; it carries the sense of solemn, witness bearing testimony. He is not giving a friendly suggestion but speaking with a charge that has the Lord's authority behind it.

The hardened heart in verse 18 is porosis, a word that began in medicine for a callus or a bone that has knitted and gone hard. Mark uses it of the people's heart in the synagogue, Mark 3:5, and Paul of Israel's partial hardening, Romans 11:25. The picture is a heart that has lost the ability to feel, and verse 19 carries the idea further. The phrase 'lost all sense of shame' translates a single participle whose root means to cease feeling pain. What once hurt the conscience no longer does. The result is aselgeia, sensuality without restraint, and pleonexia, 'a craving for more', the grasping greed that Paul links with idolatry in Ephesians 5:5.

The most important grammar is in verses 22 to 24. 'Put off' and 'put on' are aorist infinitives, which treat the act as a single decisive event, while 'be renewed' is a present infinitive, an action in progress. The change of tense gives a picture: a decisive exchange of clothes at one moment, and a daily process of renewal within. The old self is described by a present participle, 'being corrupted', an ongoing rot, in contrast with the new self which is ktisthenta, 'created', an aorist passive that points to God's act, not ours. The phrase 'according to God' tells us the new humanity is made after Him. The final pair, 'righteousness and holiness', has the second word as hosiotes, holiness, with the genitive 'of the truth', so the holiness is truth shaped, set against the 'deceitful desires' of verse 22.

Verse 26 quotes Psalm 4:4 in the Greek translation, and the verb 'be angry' is a plain imperative of concession: if you are angry, then do not sin. In verse 27 the word for foothold is topos, a place. Verse 29 describes bad talk as sapros, a word for rotten fruit or decayed fish, and sets against it oikodome, building up, the word for putting up a house, which Paul uses of the church in 4:12 and 4:16.

Verse 32 closes with a word play that English loses. The call to be 'kind' is chrestoi and to be 'tenderhearted' is eusplanchnoi, a word built on the gut, as the seat of deep feeling. 'Forgiving' is charizomenoi, from charis, grace: to forgive is to act graciously. So the believer shows grace toward others because God in Christ showed grace to us.

typology.type: Adam's image and the new humanity
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 1:26 and 27 makes humanity in God's image, and Genesis 5:3 shows Adam fathering a son in his own likeness, the image passed on, though marred. Paul pictures the new self as created like God in true righteousness and holiness, Ephesians 4:24. Christ is the true image of God, Colossians 1:15, and believers are being transformed into the same image, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The type falls short because Adam could only pass on what he had, but the last Adam gives life, 1 Corinthians 15:45, and the old self is not mended but replaced.

Scripture often uses clothes to mark a new status: Joseph's coat, priestly garments, Exodus 29:5 to 9, and the filthy robes replaced with clean ones in Zechariah 3:3 to 5. Paul takes the picture and applies it to the whole self. The putting off and putting on echoes the death and resurrection of Christ, in which the believer shares, Romans 6:4, and points toward the day the perishable puts on the imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:53. The type cannot be pushed too far, since clothing is outward and the renewal here goes to the mind and spirit.

A seal in the ancient world marked ownership and secured a thing against tampering. In Ephesians 1:13 to 14 the Spirit is the seal and the down payment of the inheritance, and here the seal looks to 'the day of redemption', when the redemption begun in Christ is completed in the resurrection of the body, Romans 8:23. The picture runs back to the way Israel was marked as God's own possession, Exodus 19:5, and the lamb's blood marking the doors at the Passover, Exodus 12:7. The seal differs from those marks in being inward and personal, the presence of God Himself.

typology.type: Forgiveness after the pattern of the cross
typology.fulfillment: The sacrificial system taught Israel that forgiveness is costly, Leviticus 4:20 and 17:11. Paul says God forgave 'in Christ', so that the cost has been paid and the forgiveness is lavish. That makes the cross both the ground of forgiveness and the pattern for believers, who are told to forgive as they have been forgiven, Colossians 3:13, and to bear one another's burdens, Galatians 6:2. The parable of the unforgiving servant, Matthew 18:23 to 35, shows how absurd it is to refuse the small debt after being freed from the great one.

study.christ:
The first and most important point is that Christ is the content of the teaching. 'You came to know Christ' in verse 20 is a striking phrase: Paul does not say they learned about Christ but that they learned Christ, as though He were the subject matter. Verse 21 deepens it: they were taught 'in Him', in the sphere of union with Him, and the truth is 'in Jesus'. It is rare for Paul to use the plain name Jesus on its own, and here it fixes the attention on the historical man whose life and cross are the standard for the new life. Everything that follows is to be read as the shape of that life.

The new self is created 'in true righteousness and holiness' because the new humanity has a head. Paul has said that the church is being built up into Christ, who is the head, Ephesians 4:15, and that He fills all things, 4:10. In the first creation God made humanity in His image; in the new creation the image is Christ Himself, 'the image of the invisible God', Colossians 1:15. To put on the new self is, in the end, to be clothed with Christ, as Romans 13:14 and Galatians 3:27 say plainly.

The practical commands carry His mark. Speaking truth because we are 'members of one another' recalls that the church is His body, 4:12 and 4:16. The refusal to leave anger overnight recalls the Man who prayed for His enemies while they crucified Him, Luke 23:34. Work that gives to the needy matches the One who, though rich, became poor so that others might be rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The speech that 'brings grace' belongs to the one whose lips were full of grace, Luke 4:22.

The Holy Spirit who is grieved by sin is the Spirit of Christ, and the sealing is Christ's gift. Ephesians 1:13 says the Spirit seals those who have believed in Him. The 'day of redemption' is the day He completes what He began.

The ending is the clearest. 'Just as in Christ God forgave you' places forgiveness at the cross. The sentence is not first of all a demand, but the reason the demand can be met. Forgiveness in Christ cost God His Son, Ephesians 1:7, and cost Christ His blood. The believer is asked only to pass on a little of what has been given in full. There is one caution: Christ is not simply an example to imitate. Paul does not say 'be like Christ and so be forgiven' but 'you have been forgiven in Christ, so be like Him'. The order is everything.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is intensely concerned with how His people live, and the reason is not that He needs rule keeping but that He is making a family in His own likeness. The new self is 'created to be like God', which tells us that righteousness and holiness are not arbitrary rules but descriptions of what God is. When a believer speaks truth, he reflects the God who does not lie, Numbers 23:19 and Titus 1:2. When he works with his hands to give to the needy, he reflects the God who opens His hand and satisfies every living thing, Psalm 145:16.

God is also the Teacher. The verbs of verses 20 and 21, 'learned', 'heard', 'were taught', show a God who forms His people through instruction in the truth, and they stand against the darkness of verse 18 where the Gentile mind is cut off from the life of God. The ignorance there is not innocent; it comes from a hardened heart. The God who calls for change is also the one who gives the light to see.

The command not to grieve the Holy Spirit is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that the Spirit is a person who can be wounded, not an impersonal force. Isaiah 63:10 gives the Old Testament root. The Spirit is not only grieved but also gives the seal, Ephesians 1:13 to 14, and so the passage holds together tender closeness and a firm guarantee. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who keeps believers safe until the day of redemption. The grief is the grief of love, not of a judge who is about to leave.

Above all, God is the one who forgives. The word translated 'forgave' is built on grace, and the sentence says the forgiveness took place 'in Christ', so that God did not forgive by turning a blind eye but by bearing the cost Himself. Justice and mercy meet in this one clause. The Father forgave, the Son was the place where it happened, and the Spirit seals the forgiven.

For worship, the passage teaches us to bring our daily speech, work and tempers before God as part of our praise. The God we adore is the God whose likeness we are being given, and the thanksgiving we offer for His forgiveness shows itself in kindness to the person who last wronged us.

crossReferences.note: The nearest parallel in the New Testament. It uses the same pair, put off and put on, with a longer list of vices and the same arrival point in forgiveness 'as the Lord forgave you'. It adds that the new self is renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator, which makes the Genesis background explicit.

The creation of humanity in God's image. Paul's 'created to be like God' echoes this passage and signals that the redemption of believers restores the purpose for which people were made in the beginning.

Paul urges believers not to be shaped by the pattern of this age but to be transformed by the renewing of the mind. It is a close match for the 'renewed in the spirit of your minds' of verse 23, and both make the mind the place where change begins.

Paul describes the nations as having become futile in their thinking, with darkened hearts. This is the same diagnosis as Ephesians 4:17 and 18, and it shows that the picture of the old life is a settled part of Paul's account of humanity apart from God.

The source of the quotation in verse 26. The psalmist addresses people who are provoked and advises them to reflect quietly rather than act. Paul uses it to show that anger itself is not the sin, but what is done with it can be.

A command to speak truth to one another, given to a people restored from exile. Paul's 'speak truthfully to his neighbor' in verse 25 echoes it and shows that honest speech is part of what marks a restored community.

Israel rebelled and grieved God's Holy Spirit, and He turned against them. It is the Old Testament root of the warning in verse 30 and shows that the Spirit's grief has long been a serious thing, not a new teaching.

The first mention of the Spirit's seal. Here the Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession. Verse 30 draws on this to show that the seal gives believers a reason to care how they live.

Jesus tells the story of a servant forgiven an enormous debt who would not forgive a small one. It is the best commentary on the final verse of the chapter, because it shows that being forgiven and forgiving are bound together.
Anyone in Christ is a new creation; the old has passed away and the new has come. Paul's language of the new self in Ephesians 4:24 is the same teaching, applied to the ethics of daily life.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with human beings made in the image of God, set in a garden to rule and fill the earth. Genesis 3 shows the image marred by distrust, and Romans 1:21 describes the effect as futility and darkened hearts. Ephesians 4:17 to 19 is that same story told of the nations in Paul's day: minds empty, hearts hard, appetites out of control. The old self is what the story calls humanity after the fall.

Into that darkness the gospel comes as a teaching and a Person. God does not merely forgive; He re-creates. The new self is 'created to be like God', and the word for 'created' is the one Scripture uses for the first creation. What was begun in Genesis is being restored in Christ, the true image of God, and the church is the first fruit of a renewed humanity. The prophets had promised that God would take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and put His Spirit within His people so that they would walk in His ways, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. Ephesians 4 is a picture of that promise being kept: the Spirit given, the mind renewed, a way of life that differs from the world.

The tension of the chapter, between a decisive change and a daily process, is the tension of the whole of Christian life between the already and the not yet. The believer has been sealed and has put on the new self, but waits for 'the day of redemption' when the work will be complete and the body itself will be raised. Until then, believers live out the new life in ordinary places, speaking truth, working honestly, settling quarrels and forgiving.

The story ends with a new creation in which nothing false or hateful will enter, Revelation 21:27, and where the redeemed will bear the likeness of Christ, 1 John 3:2. The kindness and forgiveness that Paul asks of the church now are a rehearsal for that world. Each small act of truth, work and mercy is a piece of the future, brought forward into a world that still lives in the old way.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the way of life he tells believers to abandon?

options.text: Futile in thinking, darkened in understanding, and given over to impurity.
options.note: Verses 17 to 19 describe the futile, darkened, sensual way of the Gentiles.

options.text: Wise and enlightened but simply outdated.
options.note: Paul calls it futile and darkened, not wise; it is alienated from the life of God.

options.text: Harmless and morally neutral.
options.note: It is given over to impurity with a craving for more, not neutral.

options.text: The way believers should continue to live.
options.note: Paul insists they must no longer walk this way.

quiz.q: What is the great exchange Paul describes in verses 22 to 24?

options.text: Put off the old self and put on the new self, created to be like God.
options.note: The heart of the passage is stripping off the old and clothing oneself in the new.

options.text: Trade one set of rules for another with no inner change.
options.note: The exchange includes being renewed in the spirit of the mind, not just new rules.

options.text: Improve the old self gradually while keeping it on.
options.note: The old self is to be put off, not merely improved and kept.

options.text: Wait passively for God to change everything without any response.
options.note: Believers are called to put off, be renewed, and put on.

quiz.q: What reason does Paul give for speaking truthfully to one another in verse 25?

options.text: Because we are all members of one another.
options.note: Truthful speech flows from our shared membership in the one body.

options.text: Because honesty always brings personal advantage.
options.note: The reason is our union as members of one another, not personal gain.

options.text: Because lying is merely impractical.
options.note: The deeper ground is that we belong to one another in the body.

options.text: Because the law demands it and nothing more.
options.note: Paul roots it in our new relationship as members of one body.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about anger in verses 26 and 27?

options.text: Do not sin in it, do not let it linger, and do not give the devil a foothold.
options.note: Anger must not turn to sin, fester overnight, or open a door to the devil.

options.text: All anger is sin and must be denied at once.
options.note: Paul says be angry yet do not sin, so the concern is anger that leads to sin and lingers.

options.text: Anger should be nursed and held onto as long as possible.
options.note: The command is not to let the sun set on it, the opposite of nursing it.

options.text: Anger gives no opportunity to the devil at all.
options.note: Paul warns that unresolved anger can give the devil a foothold.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by do not grieve the Holy Spirit in verse 30?

options.text: Sin pains the personal Spirit of God who indwells and seals believers.
options.note: The Spirit is a person who can be grieved, in whom we are sealed for redemption.

options.text: The Spirit is an impersonal force that cannot be affected.
options.note: Paul treats the Spirit as a person who can be grieved by sin.

options.text: We can lose the Spirit whenever we sin.
options.note: The verse stresses sealing for the day of redemption, not losing the Spirit.

options.text: The Spirit is only mildly concerned with our conduct.
options.note: The word grieve shows deep, personal concern, not mild interest.

quiz.q: On what does Paul ground the call to forgive one another in verse 32?

options.text: On the forgiveness God has shown us in Christ.
options.note: We forgive as in Christ God forgave us; grace received becomes grace given.

options.text: On the idea that the offense did not really matter.
options.note: Forgiveness releases a real wrong, grounded in God's forgiveness, not in minimizing.

options.text: On the hope that others will forgive us in return.
options.note: The ground is God's forgiveness in Christ, not a bargain with others.

options.text: On our own strength to overlook wrongs.
options.note: The motive is God's forgiving grace in Christ, not our own strength.

questions: Paul says the old way of thinking is futile and darkened. Where do you notice the leftover patterns of your old way of thinking still shaping how you live?
The new life is a great exchange: put off the old, put on the new. What is one specific thing God may be calling you to take off, and what would it look like to put on its opposite?
Verse 23 speaks of being renewed in the spirit of your mind. What are you feeding your mind, and how might God want to renew your thinking?
Paul says unresolved anger gives the devil a foothold. Is there anger you have let the sun go down on, and what would it take to deal with it before it festers?
Our words are to build others up and bring grace to those who listen. How would your speech change if that were its measure this week?
We forgive because God in Christ forgave us. Is there someone you are finding it hard to forgive, and how does remembering God's forgiveness of you help?

translationNotes.note: This verse quotes Psalm 4:4, which the Greek Old Testament renders be angry and do not sin. Paul cites it to allow that anger may arise while forbidding it to become sin or to linger; the quotation is kept with straight double quotes.
Created to be like God renders a phrase meaning created after the likeness of God, echoing the image of God in Genesis, now restored in the new self through Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 4:17-32 reproduced as supplied. The quotation of Psalm 4:4 in verse 26 is kept with straight double quotes. Inline tokens mark the seven supplied lexicon keys, each used once.
